title: API Gateway
subtitle: Centralizing edge concerns: TLS termination, JWT validation, rate limiting, routing, and the Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) pattern.
keyTakeaways: An API Gateway serves as the single public entry point for client traffic, centralizing cross-cutting concerns like TLS, authentication, and rate limiting.
The Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) pattern deploys dedicated gateways tailored to specific client platforms (iOS, Android, Web), preventing bloated one-size-fits-all payloads.
API Gateways must avoid accumulating business domain logic; gateways should focus on routing, telemetry, and protocol translation, leaving domain logic to internal services.
architectureDiagram:
BACKEND-FOR-FRONTEND (BFF) GATEWAY TOPOLOGY
[ Web Clients ]         [ Mobile iOS/Android ]         [ Third-Party APIs ]
       |                          |                               |
       v                          v                               v
[ Web BFF Gateway ]     [ Mobile BFF Gateway ]         [ Public Edge Gateway ]
(Desktop Aggregation)   (Compact JSON / Protobuf)      (Strict Rate Limiting & Auth)
       |                          |                               |
       +--------------------------+-------------------------------+
                                  |
                                  v
            [ Internal East-West Microservices Mesh ]
            (Auth Service, Order Service, Inventory Service)

sections.heading: Core Responsibilities of the Edge Gateway
sections.body: Exposing internal microservices directly to the public internet creates major security vulnerabilities, tight coupling, and excessive network round trips. An API Gateway sits between external clients and internal services, terminating connections and handling shared operational concerns.
bullets: Edge Security & Auth: Terminates TLS, validates incoming JWT tokens or API keys, and drops unauthorized traffic before it touches internal networks.
Rate Limiting & DDoS Shielding: Enforces token bucket or sliding window limits per IP or account, protecting downstream services from saturation.
Protocol Transcoding: Accepts external JSON/REST or WebSockets from browsers and translates them into internal gRPC calls over HTTP/2.
Correlation & Tracing: Injects a unique `X-Request-ID` or W3C `traceparent` header into every inbound request, ensuring end-to-end distributed trace visibility.

codeSnippet.title: API Gateway Reverse Proxy Route Definition (Envoy / KrakenD style)
codeSnippet.code:
endpoint: "/api/v1/user-dashboard"
method: "GET"
output_encoding: "json"
backend:
  - url_pattern: "/internal/v1/users/{user_id}"
    method: "GET"
    host: "http://user-service:8080"
  - url_pattern: "/internal/v1/orders/recent?user={user_id}"
    method: "GET"
    host: "http://order-service:8080"
# Concurrently queries user and order services and merges payloads into a single response

sections.heading: The Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) Pattern
sections.body: A desktop browser on high-speed fiber has different requirements than a mobile phone on a spotty cellular connection. Building a single generic API forces mobile clients to make multiple network calls to gather dashboard data, while receiving oversized JSON payloads packed with desktop-only fields. The Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) pattern creates specialized edge gateways for each client category.
bullets: Mobile BFF: Aggregates multiple backend RPC calls into a single response; strips unnecessary fields to conserve mobile bandwidth; compresses payloads.
Web BFF: Delivers rich relational payloads tailored for large screens; handles server-side rendering (SSR) session hydration.

The Antipattern of the 'Smart Gateway': Never embed business logic, database transactions, or business rules into the gateway. Gateways should remain thin routing and orchestration proxies; when gateways become bloated with domain code, they turn into monolithic bottlenecks.

tradeOffs.pros: Single operational boundary to manage; uniform security and rate limiting policies; straightforward deployment.
tradeOffs.cons: Becomes an organizational bottleneck if multiple teams fight over routing configuration; one-size-fits-all payload compromises.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Early-to-mid stage startups with uniform client requirements and smaller engineering teams.

tradeOffs.pros: Frontend teams own their respective gateways; optimal network payloads and latency per client platform; independent release cycles.
tradeOffs.cons: Operational overhead of maintaining multiple gateway fleets; potential duplication of edge authentication boilerplate.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Large engineering organizations with dedicated mobile, web, and public platform teams.

interviewTip: In mobile-heavy system design problems (like Uber or Instagram), bring up the Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) pattern: 'To optimize for lossy mobile networks, we will place a Mobile BFF Gateway between the mobile app and internal services. It aggregates multiple microservice calls into a single response and trims unneeded fields to save cellular bandwidth.'
